HEARD:
September 16 and 24, 2009

BOSWELL  J.

Introduction:

[
1
]

At one time Mr. Laszlo and Ms. Snider were actually happy together.  That
seems hard to believe now.  Their happy days are certainly long behind them.
Their current circumstances find them divorced and embroiled in a dispute in
which Mr. Laszlo alleges that Ms. Snider has alienated their two sons from him.

[
2
]

The last time Mr. Laszlo spent any meaningful time with either of his
two sons was in November 2007, when he had a visit with his son Evan, now 14.
He has not had a visit with his son, Brett, now 12, since May 2006.   According
to the terms of a Divorce Judgment dated August 6, 2004, he is a joint
custodial parent with liberal access and with “a full and active role in
providing a sound moral, social, economic and educational environment for the
children”.   In reality, he is entirely estranged from his sons and has no role
whatsoever in their lives.

[
3
]

An assessment has just been undertaken pursuant to s. 30 of the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
with a view to isolating the reasons for the estrangement
and presumably to develop a strategy to reconcile the boys with Mr. Laszlo.

[
4
]

In the meantime, Mr. Laszlo wants the parenting provisions of the
Divorce Judgment enforced.   He argues that certain relief is urgently needed
to ensure that the assessment can be meaningfully conducted and to increase the
likelihood of a successful reconciliation with his sons.

The Issues
Raised on the Motion:

[
5
]

Mr. Laszlo’s motion seeks the following specific relief:

(i)

An order compelling Ms. Snider to comply with his joint custodial and
access rights as set out in the parties’ Separation Agreement dated July 20,
2004 and the Divorce Judgment;

(ii)

In the alternative, an order prescribing significant access to be
exercised between Mr. Laszlo and the children pending completion of an
assessment report by Linda Chodos, M.S.W., R.S.W.;

(iii)

An order compelling Ms. Snider to comply in all respects with Mr.
Laszlo’s informational access rights as set out in the parties’ Separation
Agreement and the Divorce Judgment;

(iv)

A “multi-directional order” binding on the parties and a number of
specified third parties that the children of the marriage are to be referred to
as “Laszlo” and not “Snider”;

(v)

An order that Dr. Graham Berman, a psychiatrist, be retained by the
parties to conduct reunification therapy for the family, designed to reconcile
the children with Mr. Laszlo.

[
6
]

Mr. Laszlo argues that this is a classic case of parental alienation.
He says that Ms. Snider has created, by a combination of overt and subtle
actions, a culture of loathing against him which has consumed the boys,
resulting in their alienation from him.  He argues that courts must address
cases of alienation with a firm hand – that a parent who alienates a child from
another parent must be held accountable at the earliest possible opportunity.

[
7
]

There is no dispute that Mr. Laszlo’s relationship with his boys is
dismal and a long way from consistent with the provisions of the Divorce
Judgment.  Quite clearly he is estranged from the boys.   As I conclude below, Ms.
Snider has not abided by either the letter or the spirit of the Divorce
Judgment.   She has conducted herself in a manner that has undoubtedly
contributed in a substantial way to the dysfunctional relationship between Mr.
Laszlo and his sons.  But I am unable to identify her conduct as the sole cause
of the estrangement.  It appears that the current unfortunate circumstances are
the result of a constellation of factors.   The estrangement is deeply
entrenched and has prevailed for as long as three years.   The fundamental
issue on the motion, in my view, is whether the current circumstances are
amenable to an immediate litigation solution – which Mr. Laszlo advocates for -
or whether it makes more sense to pursue a therapeutic approach.

[
8
]

The motion was thoroughly and vigorously argued.   I was provided with
voluminous materials, by way of both evidence and case law.  To fully
appreciate the complexity of the issues now confronting the parties, the
children, the court and the assessor, it is necessary to review the history of
this matter from its optimistic beginnings to the grim status quo as it exists
today.  Such an overview provides an indication as to how the parties and
children came to be in the dysfunctional state they now find themselves in.  It
is necessary in order to appreciate the enormity of the task ahead of the
assessor and to understand why I believe Mr. Laszlo’s motion to be, at the very
least, premature.

The Basic
Facts:  An Optimistic Beginning:

[
9
]

The parties married one another in October 1990.   Ms. Snider was 25 at
the time and Mr. Laszlo 27.   They started a family about five years later.
Evan was their first born, on May 10, 1995.  Brett arrived almost exactly two
years later, on May 22, 1997.

[
10
]

A
separation occurred in May 2001.   From all appearances, the parties were able
to resolve the issues arising from the breakdown of their marriage in a reasonable
and sensible manner, with little conflict.   They entered into a comprehensive
Separation Agreement dated July 20, 2004.   It provided for joint custody of
the children.   Though their primary residence was to be with Ms. Snider, they
had very liberal access with Mr. Laszlo which included alternate weekends, plus
the Sunday on the off-weekend from 10:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m..   In addition,
midweek access was to alternate between Wednesday on one week and Tuesday and
Thursday on the opposite week.   Provision was also made for holiday access.

[
11
]

Paragraphs
8(e) and (f) of the Separation Agreement provide the general parenting philosophy
embraced by the parties:

(e)        It is the intention of the parties in
agreeing to joint legal custody that each of them shall continue to have a full
and active role in providing a sound moral, social, economic and educational
environment for the children and continue the support which has been provided
for the children to date.  The parents shall consult with one another in substantial
questions relating to religious upbringing, education programs, significant
changes in social environment and non-emergency health care for the children…

(f)         Each of the parents shall exert every
effort to maintain free access to and unhampered contact between the children
and the other parent and to foster a feeling of affection between the children
and the other parent   Neither parent shall do anything which would estrange
the children from the other; which would injure the opinion of the children as
to their mother or father; or which would impair the natural development of the
children’s love and respect for each of the parents.

[
12
]

Ms.
Snider commenced a divorce application in June 2004.  It proceeded
uncontested.  A Divorce Judgment was issued August 6, 2004.   It incorporated substantial portions of the Separation Agreement, including the custody
and access provisions (paragraph 8) in their entirety.    The Affidavit filed
by Ms. Snider in support of the Divorce Judgment confirmed that, as of the
Summer of 2004, access was occurring in accordance with the terms of the
Separation Agreement.

The
Estrangement:

The Restraining
Order

[
13
]

If
it were possible to pinpoint a moment when the wheels came off the bus, it
would probably be in February 2006, when Ms. Snider brought an emergency
ex
parte
motion seeking a restraining order against Mr. Laszlo.

[
14
]

According
to Ms. Snider’s Affidavit of February 17, 2006, Mr. Laszlo was still having
access with the children at that time essentially in accordance with the
Separation Agreement, save that his midweek visits were proceeding every
Wednesday only.

[
15
]

In
support of the restraining order, Ms. Snider alleged that Mr. Laszlo was
engaging in behaviour that had become increasingly harassing in nature leading
up to the sale of their former matrimonial home.   Ms. Snider’s allegations
included the following:

(i)

In September 2005, Mr. Laszlo ripped up a series of cheques and threw
them in the house, screaming that Ms. Snider was a thief, all in front of the
children;

(ii)

In December 2005, Mr. Laszlo attempted to force himself into the home
and had to be restrained by Ms. Snider’s fiancé.  The children again witnessed
the fracas.  The police were called and a CAS investigation was conducted,
including interviews of the children;

(iii)

In the several weeks leading up to the motion, Mr. Laszlo had called Ms.
Snider repeatedly on her home and cell phone – at one time calling some 40
times in a 30 minute span, witnessed by the parties’ son, Brett.

[
16
]

Ms.
Snider was granted a temporary restraining order on February 17, 2006.  It was set aside, on consent, on February 24, 2006.  In its place the parties agreed to a
mutual restraining order.   Things quickly began to deteriorate.

[
17
]

It
appears that the allegations made by Ms. Snider festered with Mr. Laszlo.   He
believed she was telling the children untruths about him.   He erupted on May 7, 2006 in an incident he described as follows:

On May 7, 2006, following the children repeating
untruths told to them by the Applicant and her husband, out of anger and
frustration I raised my voice to the children, claiming that their mother was
lying to them and that they should know better than to believe I would do such
things….

Following this outburst, on Friday May 19, 2006, the
children contacted me at work and informed me that they would not be attending
their scheduled visit with me that weekend. The children told me that the
Applicant had told them that they did not have to go with me if they did not
wish.

[
18
]

Brett
has, in fact, not attended for access with Mr. Laszlo since May 24, 2006.

Dr. Morris’
Involvement

[
19
]

To
their credit, in 2006 the parties engaged Dr. Raymond Morris, a clinical
psychologist,  with a mandate to evaluate the boys’ relationship with Mr.
Laszlo and in particular to try to improve Brett’s relationship with his
father.   Each of Mr. Laszlo, Ms. Snider and Evan had one hour sessions with
Dr. Morris.  Brett had four sessions of an hour each.   Dr. Morris released a
report dated January 16, 2007.

[
20
]

Although
Evan was not a primary focus of the clinical assignment, Dr. Morris did reflect
on his discussions with Evan as follows:

He wants to see his
father…but he has a list of concerns, which will not be outlined here.  He has
been influenced by both parents.  He knows all too well that his father blames
his mother for all of the marital problems including post-separation issues,
and his mother has shown him an email which did not reflect well on Mr.
Laszlo.  He did not feel that his father believes him in relation to his
concerns, and blames his mother for brainwashing him...

He shed some light on
Brett’s circumstance by speculating that part of the reason why Brett will not
see his father currently is because it would be perceived as a disloyalty to
his mother, despite the fact that his mother and Stephen (Mr. Snider) have
suggested that he see his father.

[
21
]

With
respect to Brett, Dr. Morris reviewed a series of incidents reported by Brett
that justified, in Brett’s mind, the breakdown of his relationship with his
father.   Brett suggested that his father was mean and favoured Evan, that his
father spoke badly of his mother and that he had been exposed to a number of
his father’s female friends.  He placed particular emphasis on an incident when
Ms. Snider was not home and Mr. Laszlo pushed his way into the home and took
pictures off the wall.    Brett expressed anger at his father for behaviour
which was offensive to him and clearly aligned to his mother to whom he is
extremely closely attached.

[
22
]

Dr.
Morris confirmed the obvious:  the boys had been subject to parental conflict
and tension to a degree that had not been in their best interest.  The boys had
reacted differently because of their ages and differences in their
personalities.   Brett’s preference not to see his father was based, he said, on
his own personal experience of not being favoured or prized in a way he would
like.

[
23
]

Dr.
Morris made recommendations.  He said the situation between the boys and Mr.
Laszlo would not improve unless:

1.

Exposure to parental conflict ceased;

2.

Mr. Laszlo stopped bad-mouthing Ms. Snider;

3.

The boys were made a priority in Mr. Laszlo’s life and not exposed to
his computer dating and involvement with other women;

4.

The boys were not shown anything relating to parental conflict;

5.

The boys were not only given permission to see their father but told
they should do so in their best interest.  Their choice should be removed.

[
24
]

It
was suggested that Mr. Laszlo start out slowly by sending Brett holiday cards
and explain his understanding and concern for Brett’s issues.  Subsequently an
invitation to something Brett really wanted to go to could be extended and the
relationship rebuilt around mutually enjoyable experiences.

[
25
]

Notwithstanding
the work done by Dr. Morris and his recommendations, there was no
reconciliation between Brett and Mr. Laszlo.   In fact, things worsened.

The July 2007 Motion

[
26
]

In
the face of a breakdown in the access arrangements, Mr. Laszlo applied, in July
2007, for an order appointing a parenting coordinator, confirming his access
and prohibiting Ms. Snider from making unilateral decisions regarding the
children’s education, religious activities or extra-curricular programs.

[
27
]

In
his affidavit sworn July 6, 2007, Mr. Laszlo claimed that Ms. Snider was
unilaterally making decisions about the children’s day-to-day activities and
had effectively alienated him from his children’s lives.    He said the
following:

The Applicant’s refusal to involve me in all
decisions pertaining to the children’s lives has significantly contributed to
the current breakdown of the relationship and communication between me and my
children.  The children have been made to believe that my views, opinions and
thoughts are unnecessary, irrelevant and deliberately destructive.  My children
no longer consider me as a source of potential advice, support and guidance.

[
28
]

Following
the restraining order motion in February 2006, the escalation in conflict
between Ms. Snider and Mr. Laszlo quickly emerged as a conflict between the
children (primarily Brett) and Mr. Laszlo.  Mr. Laszlo was by no means innocent
in the escalation of conflict.  But email correspondence between the parties
vividly demonstrates that Ms. Snider worked up the conflict and supported the
rift between Brett and his father.  While she may genuinely have thought that
she was supporting Brett’s emotional needs, what she was unfortunately doing
was supporting Brett’s immature and ineffective way of addressing issues with
his father.   Even more unfortunate is the fact that the issues were really
matters of conflict between the parents and the boys ought to have been
insulated from them.

[
29
]

In
essence, the July 2007 motion demonstrated that conflicts had arisen between
the parents and their joint custodial arrangement had broken down.  As Mr.
Laszlo became more isolated from the boys the level of conflict increased.  The
boys allied themselves with their mother.  She did not insulate them, nor
direct them appropriately.  Instead she embraced their issues with Mr. Laszlo
and supported them because doing so was consistent with her negative view of
Mr. Laszlo.

[
30
]

The
motion materials filed in connection with the July 2007 motion include substantial
email correspondence between the parties.  A flavour of the dynamic between
them emerges from the emails:

(i)

On June 7, 2006 Mr. Laszlo asked Ms. Snider to provide him with a copy
of Brett’s baseball schedule, as it appeared that many of Brett’s games
occurred on scheduled access dates.

(ii)

In response Ms. Snider said, “Brett has asked me NOT to provide this
specific information to you and I fully intend to respect his wishes.   I
strongly suggest you do the same….Moreover, as he has REPEATEDLY expressed to
you, he does not want to be bound to see you by any set schedule.  He has many
friends, parties and activities he wants to be involved with.  He has the right
to decide who he wants to involve in those….I truly fail to understand why you
can’t see that the children are no longer babies.  Hanging out with parents is
not something that should (or can) be forced on them anymore….If you persist in
attempting to force or pressure Brett to see or involve you against his wishes,
regardless of whether or not it is on your scheduled day, please be advised
that I have every intention of getting involved in full legal proceedings to
protect his wishes.”    It is important to note that Brett was 9 years old at
the time of this email exchange.

(iii)

Mr. Laszlo countered with, “I appreciate your comments, although I do not
completely agree with them.  Whether you agree or not, I have a legal right to
see the children on certain days and on those days, you should not be setting
up plans for the children and agreeing to arrange activities for them before
you or they have consulted with me….Although the children are growing up and
are involved in a broader range of activities, they are still children and must
still abide to the wishes of their parents.  I don’t feel that suggesting that
the children are free to come and go as they please without my permission or
even informing me is respectful and something they should be taught.”

(iv)

Some of the highlights of Ms. Snider’s reply are as follows:

•

“[T]he children have a legal right not to be forced to see you at
their own request.”

•

“I can not and will not abide by your request that I not arrange
parties or activities for the children on your scheduled days/nights.  This is
completely irrational and ludicrous.”

•

“As it always has been, and obviously always will be, you totally
disregarded and completely ignored the message of my email, which was the
FEELINGS OF BRETT….Because Brett had asked me to write you about his feelings,
I allowed him to read your response.  He was stunned, angered and frustrated by
your response.”

(v)

On June 29, 2006, Ms. Snider emailed Mr. Laszlo about Brett’s baseball.
Evidently Mr. Laszlo had attended one of Brett’s ball games, despite having
been advised that Brett did not want him there.   Ms. Snider warned, “I have
spoken with the Executive Board of the Thornhill Baseball league, the league
convenor, his team coaches, the police and my lawyer regarding your attendance
against Brett’s express wishes at his baseball game on Tuesday June 27 at Grandview
Park.  They are now aware of this situation.”

(vi)

A particularly sore point for Mr. Laszlo relates to the arrangements for
Evan’s Bar Mitzvah.   Both parties are Jewish and the children have been raised
in the Jewish faith.   The Bar Mitzvah is the coming of age ceremony for a 13
year old Jewish boy and in Evan’s case was a ceremony of some significance to
both Ms. Snider and Mr. Laszlo.   On July 19, 2006 Ms. Snider sent Mr. Laszlo
an email notifying him that she and Mr. Snider (her new spouse) and the boys
were now members of Temple Kol Ami and that the boys would be starting Hebrew School
there in the Fall of 2006.   She advised that Evan’s Bar Mitzvah had been
booked for May 31, 2008 at Temple Kol Ami.   Mr. Laszlo had not been consulted
about the change in synagogues, the enrolment in Hebrew School, or about the
arrangements for the Bar Mitzvah itself, despite the provisions of paragraph
8(e) of the Divorce Judgment.   At this time, although access with Brett had
stopped, access was continuing to occur between Mr. Laszlo and Evan.

(vii)

A dispute arose between the parties about a trip Ms. Snider planned to
take the children on to Florida in March 2007.   Mr. Laszlo was reluctant to provide
a consent to the travel.   The children were informed of his position.  Evan
and Brett sent the following email to Mr. Laszlo that can only be described as
disturbing:

Just
to let you know, I will not be seeing you today unless you sign it takes 2 second
out of your life is that such a problem?  I would do it and a normal dad will
too.  And if u don’t do it, I will not ever see u like brett mostly likely.
Now it’s brett.  SIGN the FRIGEN THING!!! IT ISNT HARD a 2 year old can do that
hahahahahahaha lol so I guess your a baby then!!!! hahahaha u cant even sign a
piece of paper ahhahahaahhaahhahah sign it or im never no matter what even if u
uy me 20 convertibles see you again or talking to you again or looking at u
again so sign it!!!! Sign it right when u get this at your grose apartment and
sign it or evan is never seeing u again or talking to u because your running
are lives so sign it now so too bad for u too bad so sad.

[
31
]

The
email correspondence between the parties demonstrates clearly that Ms. Snider
had little regard for the parenting provisions found in either the Separation
Agreement or the Divorce Judgment.

The Office of the
Children’s Lawyer

[
32
]

At
a Case Conference on December 17, 2007, the parties consented to an order that
the Office of the Children’s Lawyer (“OCL”) be asked to provide assistance in
this matter.   Subsequently, the OCL elected to appoint counsel for the boys -
Ms. D. Herriot-Howes.

[
33
]

Ms.
Herriot-Howes held a disclosure meeting with the parties in February 2009. She told
them Brett had no interest in reconciling with Mr. Laszlo, but Evan was
prepared to engage in reconciliation counselling.   Unfortunately, it appears
that the parties were not able to agree on whether such counselling should
proceed.

The March 2008
Motion

[
34
]

Despite
the fact that Brett had not gone for access with his father since May 2006 and
Ms. Snider’s position that the children need not visit Mr. Laszlo if they
didn’t want to, it was not until March 2008 that she moved to vary the Divorce
Judgment.  She sought an order for sole custody of the boys, together with a
provision for access commensurate with the wishes of the children.

[
35
]

She
filed an affidavit sworn February 18, 2008.  In it she said that she and Mr.
Laszlo had many difficulties communicating before the Separation Agreement was
signed.  Nevertheless, it was her “fervent hope” that by agreeing to a joint
custody regime, the two of them would be able to co-parent effectively.

[
36
]

Ms.
Snider explained that joint parenting had not worked, for reasons which included
the following:

(i)

Mr. Laszlo did not respect her and denigrated her continuously to the
children and to the community;

(ii)

Mr. Laszlo did not encourage the children’s relationship with her;

(iii)

Mr. Laszlo posted a comment on his Facebook profile to the effect that
Ms. Snider was alienating him from the children;

(iv)

Mr. Laszlo did not respect her exclusive possession of the former
matrimonial home and routinely entered it without her permission;

(v)

Mr. Laszlo sent her an email in December 2004 in which he said, “keep in
mind that for as much as you hate me, I despise you even more and the thought
that I have to deal with you at all absolutely repulses me to the point that it
truly makes me sick to my stomach”.

[
37
]

Ms.
Snider opined that Mr. Laszlo has serious mental health problems, including
depression and a personality disorder.  He is self-absorbed and unable to
empathize with other’s feelings.   She described the incident that led to the
cessation of access between Brett and Mr. Laszlo, in May 2006, as follows:

On the Sunday of the
weekend access, [Mr. Laszlo] screamed and yelled at the children for literally
hours and hours.  The yelling was so bad that [Mr. Laszlo’s] neighbours were
banging on his walls.   [Mr. Laszlo] told the children that they had lied and
ruined his life.   [He] referred to me as a “fucking liar” and “bitch”.  He
said my husband was violent and was going to harm them.  He said that my
husband pays for nothing and that he pays for things in their lives.  He said
repeatedly that all my husband cared about was “fucking baseball”…

[
38
]

She
went on to say that the children were visibly shaken and upset when they
returned from the access visit and that they were afraid of Mr. Laszlo after
that time.

[
39
]

She
said that she has tried providing Mr. Laszlo with suggestions about how to deal
with Brett, but nevertheless, Mr. Laszlo has continued to distance and alienate
himself from Brett by his behaviour.  Her description of his poor behaviour was
hardly compelling:

(i)

he has lifted Brett like a young child, which has humiliated him;

(ii)

he has disregarded what Brett has told him;

(iii)

he has refused to provide Brett with his bike;

(iv)

he attended at Brett’s baseball games despite Brett’s wishes.

The Assessment

[
40
]

Ms.
Snider’s motion to vary access and Mr. Laszlo’s motion to confirm his rights as
a joint custodial parent were both adjourned.  I understand the parties were
awaiting input from the OCL before proceeding further.  Subsequently, they
agreed to engage in a psychological assessment pursuant to s. 30 of the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
.  The scope of the assessment is interesting.  The assessor
is mandated to address two issues:

1.

The validity of Mr. Laszlo’s allegation of alienation of the children by
Ms. Snider and, if substantiated, the nature and effect of the mother’s actions
in this regard; and,

2.

Whether Mr. Laszlo has narcissistic traits that impact on his ability to
parent the children and to what extent the behaviour and actions of Mr. Laszlo
contributed to his estrangement from the children.

The May 2009
Motion

[
41
]

Although
able to agree on the concept of an assessment, the parties were unable to agree
on the assessor.  Mr. Laszlo moved in May 2009 for the direction of the court
as to who would conduct the assessment.

[
42
]

In
support of his motion Mr. Laszlo filed an affidavit dated May 2, 2009.   He
described his co-parenting arrangement with Ms. Snider as deteriorating rapidly
after she commenced a relationship with Mr. Snider in early 2005.  He said that
“despite my continual efforts to foster a more cooperative co-parenting stance on
the part of the Applicant, she began to undermine my relationship first with my
son Brett and, subsequently, with my son Evan.”

[
43
]

Mr.
Laszlo’s affidavit blamed the cessation of access visits with his sons on Ms.
Snider and characterized the lack of access as a breach of the Divorce Judgment
her.   He said the children have been encouraged to look to Mr. Snider as their
new father, with Brett going so far as to wear the name “Snider” on the back of
his sports jerseys.  He complained that his entire extended family, including
the children’s grandparents, cousins and others have been wiped out of the
children’s lives.  Mr. Laszlo asserted that “this is a classic case of parental
alienation”.

[
44
]

Mr.
Laszlo asked that Dr. Sol J. Goldstein be appointed to conduct the assessment.
As an alternative to Dr. Goldstein, seven other individuals were suggested as
possible assessors.   Dr. Goldstein is a psychiatrist who was offered as an
expert in parental alienation.   He has apparently been qualified to give
expert evidence in the Province of Ontario, but it is not clear to me what
particular field of expertise he has been qualified in.   His
Curriculum
Vitae
indicates that he has been involved in some 500 assessments,
mediations and treatments of divorcing families since 1968 but does not contain
any reference to an expertise in parental alienation.

[
45
]

The
term “parental alienation syndrome” was coined by an American psychiatrist, Dr.
Richard Gardner, to describe what he referred to as a medical disorder.
Parental alienation syndrome is not formally recognized as a medical disorder
and does not appear in the DSM-IV.   There is disagreement in the medical
profession as to whether it is properly characterized as a disorder.  That
said, there can be little dispute that parental alienation exists as a dynamic
in some divorcing families, involving the estrangement of a child from a
parent.

[
46
]

Ms.
Snider dismissed Dr. Goldstein as an assessor.  Mr. Laszlo complained that Ms.
Snider had rejected
all
of his suggested assessors as being professionals
inclined to support parental alienation as a disorder.  In the meantime, Ms.
Snider suggested four other possible assessors, all of whom were rejected by
Mr. Laszlo.  One of Ms. Snider’s proposed assessors was Dr. Graham Berman. Significantly,
Mr. Laszlo rejected Dr. Berman, saying that Ms. Snider had “failed to
demonstrate that he has the requisite knowledge and clinical experience to deal
with concerns about the Applicant’s alienation of his children from him.”
Moreover, Mr. Laszlo cited a court decision in which Dr. Berman was criticized
by the court.  An assessment report he had authored was described by the court
as neither complete nor impartial.

[
47
]

The
parties ultimately agreed upon Linda Chodos as the assessor.  She was suggested
by Mr. Laszlo.

The Current Motion

[
48
]

The
assessment process is just now underway.   Mr. Laszlo’s counsel expressed
concern that it may be many months before a report is completed, with many more
months after that before a trial can be conducted, should the parties not be
able to reach a resolution with the assessor’s assistance.

[
49
]

Mr.
Laszlo’s motion, he argues, is brought for the purpose of reinforcing the
necessity of Ms. Snider’s compliance with the prevailing court order and to
address certain factors that are of significant importance to the ability of
the assessor to conduct a full and fair inquiry into the issues that form her
mandate.

[
50
]

It
is important to note that although Mr. Laszlo is seeking an order enforcing the
parenting terms of the Divorce Judgment, he has not sought a finding of
contempt.  Rather, his motion asks that Ms. Snider be “compelled to comply with
[Mr. Laszlo’s] joint custody and access rights”.   The balance of specific
relief sought is set out in paragraph 3 above.

[
51
]

In
support of his motion, Mr. Laszlo filed an affidavit sworn August 20, 2009.  He
describes the goal of the motion at paragraphs 31 to 33 of the affidavit:

31

[M]y goal in bringing this Motion is to lay the foundation for the
reconciliation of myself and my children.  Urgent and strong steps need to be
taken as a result of the lost time over the past two to three years.

32

The current family dynamic has festered into a dysfunctional stalemate
which has seen the estrangement fostered by the Applicant solidify and suffer
from inertia.

33

The Applicant has been in blatant contempt of court for over three years
and has done everything possible to throw roadblocks in the way of
reconciliation.

[
52
]

Again,
although Mr. Laszlo’s affidavit specifically refers to contempt and although his
counsel, Mr. Ludmer, repeatedly referred to alleged contumacious conduct on the
part of Ms. Snider, the motion does not seek a finding of contempt.  Having not
been asked to make a finding of contempt, no such finding will be made.   The
allegations of contempt will remain just that – allegations.

(i)

The August 20, 2009 affidavit otherwise repeats much of the information
found in Mr. Laszlo’s July 2007 affidavit.

[
53
]

Dr.
Goldstein provided an affidavit sworn August 19, 2009 in support of Mr.
Laszlo’s motion.  He offered the following opinions:

(i)

The fact that Ms. Snider and her new husband refer to the children as
“Snider” will be a powerful and direct impediment to the reconciliation of the
children with Mr. Laszlo;

(ii)

A “multi-directional order” should be made compelling the parties and
third parties to refer to the children as “Laszlo” and to Mr. Laszlo as “Dad”;

(iii)

Normal parent-child social activities should be immediately recommenced;
and,

(iv)

Therapeutic intervention by a qualified mental health professional with
experience in dealing with cases of extreme estrangement of children is also
required immediately.

[
54
]

Ms.
Snider responded to Mr. Laszlo’s August 20, 2009 affidavit with an affidavit of
her own, sworn September 8, 2009.  She too repeated much of the information
filed in earlier material.

[
55
]

Ms.
Snider filed an affidavit from Dr. Leonard Feldman, a psychiatrist related to
her.  He was critical of Dr. Goldstein’s affidavit, saying his opinions were
not supported with a proper documentary review, that his language was not
neutral and that the affidavit in general was not in keeping with the
guidelines of the College of Physicians and Surgeons relating to third party
reports.

[
56
]

Mr.
Laszlo responded vigorously.   He filed a reply affidavit sworn September 13,
2009, together with the affidavits of friends supporting his position.  He also
filed a supplemental affidavit of Dr. Goldstein sworn September 12, 2009.   Dr.
Goldstein opined that it was not appropriate for Dr. Feldman to provide input
into this case because he is a relative of Ms. Snider.   He went on to say that
he has not provided an expert’s report in this case, but rather has made
general observations based on forty years of experience.

[
57
]

Dr.
Goldstein affirmed his position regarding the name change and went on to say
that, based on his review of Ms. Snider’s allegations against Mr. Laszlo, there
are no concerns of such a magnitude that danger to the children is a factor.
He said that the validity of the assessment process will be enhanced if the
assessor has some normalized current interactions between father and sons to
form part of her observations and analysis.  He reiterated that firm direction
from the court is required along with family reconciliation and, if needed,
restriction on the children’s exposure to Ms. Snider, until they can develop
the necessary critical thinking skills to regularize their relationship with
Mr. Laszlo.

Discussion of
the Outstanding Issues:

[
58
]

Evan
and Brett are estranged from Mr. Laszlo and they are entrenched in their
positions.  Mr. Laszlo has contributed to the estrangement.   He made mistakes
after the separation.  He appears to have, at least at times, put his own need
for companionship ahead of his children’s interests.  He contributed to
conflict with Ms. Snider and in the course of that conflict, the children
aligned themselves with their mother.  The children are now deprived of a
relationship with their father, but in circumstances where none of the
allegations made by Ms. Snider would, in my view, justify the termination of
the relationship.

[
59
]

Though
Mr. Laszlo has contributed to the current dysfunctional situation, it is Ms.
Snider’s conduct that is its primary cause.   It is largely her behaviour, both
subtle and blatant, that has contributed to the breakdown of the relationship
between Mr. Laszlo and his children.   She has, at times, been merely complicit
in the estrangement, but at other times has been very actively cultivating it.

[
60
]

I
point to the following factors, as set out more particularly above:

(i)

The suggestion that a nine year old child can dictate when and if he
will go for access visits with his father is wrong.  Ms. Snider appears to have
put Brett’s interest in spending time with his friends above the importance of
maintaining a relationship with his father.  The parties decided that it was in
his best interests to maintain a joint parenting arrangement with substantial
access with his father.  She should have required that he comply with the
visitation agreed upon.  Instead, she empowered him to make the choice and in
doing so, effectively ensured that the choice would be not to go;

(ii)

The argument that Brett had a legal right not to go for access visits
flies in the face of the court ordered access regime;

(iii)

Showing Brett adult email correspondences, centered on the conflict
between the parties, was unconscionable.  It was harmful to Brett.  He was
stunned, angered and frustrated.   Any sensible parent does his or her best to
insulate their children from conflict and harm.   She engaged the children in
it;

(iv)

She planned activities for the children on scheduled access dates
without consultation with Mr. Laszlo, then suggested it was ludicrous for him
to complain;

(v)

Her behaviour surrounding the baseball issue was just simply irrational
and nothing more than a manufactured crisis;

(vi)

She has allowed, if not encouraged, Brett to adopt the name “Snider”.
Her protestation that she was powerless as a parent to prevent this young boy
from expressing “his” desire to be a Snider rings hollow.   I can not believe
that she has such little influence or control over her children;

(vii)

She has demonstrated a blatant disregard for the provisions of the
Divorce Judgment that require consultation and the involvement of both parents
in important issues relating to the children.   The unilateral change in places
of worship and the exclusion of Mr. Laszlo from the planning of Evan’s Bar
Mitvah are just two examples.

[
61
]

Ms.
Snider clearly holds a view of Mr. Laszlo’s role as a parent as marginal,
despite the clear intention otherwise expressed in the Separation Agreement and
Divorce Judgment.   It is not surprising that the children hold the same view.

[
62
]

Having
said all of that, the best interests of the children remain the sole focus of
the court at this time.   This is not a contempt motion, which would otherwise
engage issues focused on the integrity of the court and its processes.  This is
a motion relating solely to the children’s relationship with Mr. Laszlo and
that means that the children’s best interests govern.

[
63
]

Despite
my view, as expressed, that Ms. Snider is largely to blame for the current
estrangement, the circumstances are complex and Mr. Laszlo is not without
culpability here.  The situation is entrenched.  It has been years since Mr.
Laszlo has seen the children – two years in the case of Evan, more than three
in the case of Brett.   The boys, who are now 12 and 14, have expressed that
they do not wish to have a relationship with their father.   Their views and
preferences must be given some consideration.

[
64
]

The
parties have themselves agreed that an assessment is appropriate to determine
the causes of the alienation and potential fixes.  That assessment is just now
underway.   OCL counsel submitted that the motion is premature and should await
the outcome of the assessment and for the most part I agree, despite Dr.
Goldstein’s expressed views to the contrary.

[
65
]

Having
made those general comments, I will now specifically review the relief
requested in Mr. Laszlo’s motion.

(i)         Compelling
Access Pending the Assessment:

[
66
]

The
Divorce Judgment contains a specified access schedule.   It has not been
adhered to.   Mr. Laszlo wants it enforced.  His evidence is replete with
references to contempt.  His lawyer filed with the court numerous cases dealing
with the issue of contempt.   But there is no contempt motion before the court.
Such a motion would engage fundamental issues relating to the integrity of the
court process and respect for the administration of justice.  It would require
proof beyond a reasonable doubt – a standard the current record does not meet,
given the complex circumstances surrounding the estrangement.

[
67
]

Mr.
Ludmer confirmed that this is not a contempt motion.  In his words, it is a
“compliance” motion.  What is sought is an order that, notwithstanding the
prevailing circumstances, Ms. Snider must follow the provisions of the Divorce
Judgment.  Presumably this is a precursor to a contempt motion.   An order that
tells Ms. Snider that she must comply with the provisions of the access
schedule notwithstanding the current difficult circumstances, may preclude her
from relying on those circumstances in a follow-up contempt motion.  The issue
now is whether the importance of compliance with the outstanding order should,
in effect, trump all other circumstances.

[
68
]

Mr.
Ludmer argues that a failure to insist on immediate compliance with the access
schedule set out in the Divorce Judgment would essentially condone Ms. Snider’s
breach and foster disrespect for the court’s processes.  He placed significant
emphasis on the recent case of
Sickinger v. Sickinger
[1]
,

a 2009 decision of Madam Justice Greer.  He went so far as to have Mr.
Sickinger appear in court to apparently lend moral support to the cause.   In
Sickinger
,
Justice Greer made an order compelling a mother to comply with the access
provisions for a sixteen year old daughter who had been estranged from her
father for more than half a year.  Justice Greer found that Ms. Sickinger had
failed to comply with the provisions of a court ordered access schedule, even
though the child was saying that she didn’t want to go for visits with her
father.  In finding the mother in contempt of the existing order, Greer, J.
followed the decision of Reilly, J. in
V. (S) v.
I.
(T.)
[2]
holding that a  parent does not have to force a child to go for court
ordered access, but should "require" the child to go.  A failure to
require the child to do that is considered contempt.

[
69
]

While
I agree with Mr. Ludmer that compliance with court orders is not optional, the
issue of enforcement in the particular circumstances of this case is complex.
It would be naïve to pretend that there has not been a significant shift in the
parenting dynamic since the Divorce Judgment was made.  Quite clearly there are
difficult issues to struggle with now, that did not exist when the Divorce
Judgment was issued.   In particular:

(i)

There is clearly an estrangement between Mr. Laszlo and the boys.
There is at least some evidence to suggest that non-compliance with the
Judgment is the result of the choices made by the children;

(ii)

There is an assessment just now underway to inquire into the reasons for
the non-compliance with the order, the reasons for the estrangement and how
best to reconcile the children with their father;

(iii)

There is an outstanding motion to vary the Judgment; and,

(iv)

The Office of the Children’s Lawyer has appointed counsel for the
children.   Ms. Herriot-Howes advised the court that both boys expressed
reluctance to have a relationship with Mr. Laszlo, but their reasons were
disproportionate to the strength of their convictions.  She expressed concerns
about the independence of the children’s views.   Nevertheless, the position
advanced by Ms. Herriot-Howes was that Mr. Laszlo’s motion was premature and
that the best course of action is to let the assessment run its course.

[
70
]

Regardless
of the altered parenting dynamic present here, Mr. Ludmer argues that the
reasoning in
Sickinger
should be applied and the children should
immediately be required to attend for access in accordance with the Divorce
Judgment.

[
71
]

While
I do not take issue with the reasoning in
Sickinger
, the case now before
the court has significant differences from the facts in
Sickinger
.
In
particular:

(i)
Sickinger
was a contempt motion.   A
finding of contempt was made.  That is not the case here;

(ii)        There has been a longer period of estrangement
here.  Mr. Sickinger had been estranged from his daughter for some eight months
or so.   Mr. Laszlo has not seen Brett since the Spring of 2006 and Evan since
the Fall of 2007.   The dynamic is now much more entrenched than it was in
Sickinger

and that much more difficult to fix;

(iii)       Both children have been completely estranged
from Mr. Laszlo.  Only one of three children was estranged from Mr. Sickinger;

(iv)

There is an assessment just getting underway in this instance; and,

(v)

The circumstances here are much more nuanced.   Ms. Snider claims that
she has encouraged access.   Mr. Laszlo is at least partly to blame for the
estrangement - the report of Dr. Morris confirms as much. The specific mandate
given to the assessor demonstrates that the causes and cures of the
estrangement are complex.

[
72
]

The
current order is clearly not being followed, but I do not see this as a case
where the best interests of the children will be advanced by an order saying
that, after three years of no access, the children must immediately begin to
follow the provisions of the Divorce Judgment.  Mr. Laszlo acknowledges that
there is no easy fix and that, at the very least, reconciliation counselling
will be required.   His expert, Dr. Goldstein, is of the same view.  The
situation is now too textured and complex to resolve by blindly insisting on
the children’s compliance with the Divorce Judgment.  In my view, the complex
and difficult access issues between the parties should be deferred until the
assessment is completed.

[
73
]

I
appreciate that my finding is at odds with the views expressed by Dr.
Goldstein.  He was firmly of the view that the recommencement of access should
not wait until the assessment is completed.  In his affidavit of September 12,
2009, Dr. Goldstein opined that the reconciliation of Mr. Laszlo with his sons
requires immediate recommencement of normal parent-child social activities.  This
is so, he said, for several reasons, including:

(i)

the validity of the assessment process will be enhanced if the assessor
has some normalized current interactions between father and sons to form part
of her observations and analysis.

(ii)

with the overall family dynamic less deadlocked, the assessor, and
therapists working with the family in parallel, will have more freedom to
investigate causes, effects and remedies for the family.

(iii)

the tools available for intervention in these circumstances are few and
therefore need not wait.  Those tools are limited to:  significant and firm
direction from the court as to the support the mother must show for the sons’ relationship
with their father; family reconciliation therapy and related education;  and, if
needed, restrictions on the children’s exposure to Ms. Snider.

[
74
]

At
the end of the day, Dr. Goldstein may be right.  The assessment process may be
enhanced by the steps he suggests.   But it must be remembered that he was
rejected as the assessor in this matter.   Ms. Linda Chodos will be conducting
the assessment.  There was no evidence from her regarding any court
intervention she considers necessary in order to be in a position to complete
her work.   She may agree with Dr. Goldstein.  She may not.    To simply follow
Dr. Goldstein’s recommendations without input from Ms. Chodos, would permit Dr.
Goldstein to usurp the assessment process.

[
75
]

In
the result, I decline to make any order at this time regarding access.  The
Divorce Order remains outstanding.   Whether there is to be a variation of its
access terms, or whether steps should be taken to enforce its terms, are issues
to be deferred until evidence is received from the assessor regarding the
causes of the estrangement, with recommendations for reconciliation strategies.

(ii)        Informational
Rights

[
76
]

The
parties continue to have joint custody of the boys.  The Divorce Judgment
contains provisions respecting consultation with one another on substantial
questions relating to the children.
[3]

Ms. Snider has not complied with these provisions.  The unilateral decision to
change the children’s place of worship is but one example.  She must comply
immediately.  Whatever the reasons are for the estrangement, they should not
prevent Mr. Laszlo from being fully informed – as a joint custodial parent
should be – about the children’s lives.   In addition to the specific
provisions of the Divorce Judgment, Mr. Laslzo is to be provided, on a
continuing basis, with all material information relating to the health,
education and welfare of both boys.

(iii)       Name
Change

[
77
]

The
surnames of the children have not been legally changed, nor could they be, in
light of the Divorce Judgment, without Mr. Laszlo’s consent.  It appears that,
for all intents and purposes, Brett has adopted the surname “Snider”.  Ms.
Snider has, at the very least acquiesced in Brett’s change in surname.   She
should not have done so.   The record before me does not disclose a sufficient
basis on which I could find that it is in Brett’s best interests that his
surname be changed, whether formally or
de facto
.   Ms. Snider shall
immediately refrain from referring to Brett as “Snider” and she shall refer to
him as “Laszlo.”   Moreover, she is to require Brett to use the name “Laszlo”.

[
78
]

Mr.
Laszlo asked for a “multi-directional” order parroting language used by Dr.
Goldstein.  The attempt is to bind non-parties who were not privy to this
motion to the order regarding the children’s last name.  I will not make such
an order in the absence of notice to any party to be bound by it.

(iv)       Reunification
Therapy

[
79
]

Mr.
Laszlo asks that an order be made that the children participate in
reunification therapy with Dr. Graham Berman.   Dr. Goldstein strongly suggests
it.   Ms. Snider resists any order which would compel the children to be in
counselling while the assessment is underway, save and except as may be
recommended by the assessor.  The OCL takes a position similar to that of Ms.
Snider.

[
80
]

While
the court has the inherent jurisdiction to order reconciliation counselling,
such orders are made sparingly:
Kramer v. Kramer
.
[4]

There should be compelling evidence that the counselling will be beneficial to
the participants.

[
81
]

The
likely benefit must certainly be questioned where, as here, the counselling is
resisted by three of the four proposed participants.  That said, resistance can
not and should not be the sole determining factor when the welfare of the
children is in issue.  It is not difficult to envision circumstances where the
court may be justified in imposing counselling, even though there is opposition
to it.   But I come back to the fact that there is an assessment just
underway.  I believe  it will be greatly beneficial to have the views and
findings of the assessor before imposing any particular form of counselling on
the parties and the children.

[
82
]

Even
if I were inclined to impose counselling at this time, which I am not, I
certainly would not direct that the counselling be with Dr. Berman.  His
credentials were thoroughly impugned by Mr. Laszlo.  According to Mr. Laszlo’s
own evidence, Dr. Berman lacks the requisite knowledge and clinical experience
to deal with concerns about the alienation of Mr. Laszlo’s children from him.
It makes little sense to appoint a counselor in whom Mr. Laszlo has such little
faith.

[
83
]

In
the result, save for the orders set out in paragraphs 77 and 78 herein, Mr.
Laszlo’s motion is dismissed.  Mr. Laszlo shall, however, be at liberty to
re-apply for the relief set out in his motion upon receipt of a report from the
assessor, Linda Chodos.
